entries.question: Did David sin?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 22:21-25 has David claiming the LORD rewarded him according to his righteousness and the cleanness of his hands. 1 Kings 15:5 says David did right "all the days of his life, save only in the matter of Uriah." 2 Samuel 24:10 and 1 Chronicles 21:8 have David confessing he sinned greatly in numbering the people. So at least three answers exist within the canon: none, one (Uriah), and at least two (Uriah plus the census).
entries.commentary:
The three texts answer the same question — did David sin? — in three incompatible ways. 2 Samuel 22, paralleled in Psalm 18, is a victory psalm where David sings about his own righteousness in absolute terms: clean hands, righteousness, no departure from God's statutes. Read at face value, this is David saying he hasn't sinned. 1 Kings 15:5 is a deuteronomistic editorial summary that gives the qualified answer — David was righteous except in the Uriah affair. 2 Samuel 24:10 and 1 Chronicles 21:8 introduce a second confessed sin, the census.

The standard harmonization is that 2 Samuel 22 is a piece of liturgical poetry written before the Bathsheba and census incidents, or that David is speaking comparatively (righteous compared to Saul), or that "cleanness of hands" refers to specific contexts (his treatment of Saul) rather than his entire moral record. There is something to the comparative-righteousness reading — the psalm is set in the context of David's deliverance from his enemies, and the immediate referent is probably his behavior toward Saul. But the language is unqualified: "according to my righteousness ... according to the cleanness of my hands ... in his eye sight." Not "compared to Saul." Not "in this matter." The psalmist's voice is making a categorical claim.

1 Kings 15:5 then explicitly carves out the Uriah exception — which means the Deuteronomist who wrote that summary considered the Uriah affair David's only sin. He didn't say "except for Uriah and the census." He said only Uriah. So either the Deuteronomist didn't know the census story, didn't count it as a sin, or considered Uriah categorically worse. 2 Samuel 24 and 1 Chronicles 21 both treat the census as a confessed sin, so the canon as a whole records at least two sins, but 1 Kings 15:5 reports only one.

The critical reading is that these texts come from different hands with different agendas. The Deuteronomistic Historian's summary in 1 Kings 15:5 is designed to make David the standard against which later Judean kings are measured, and the Uriah affair is the only stain he allows on the standard. Different authors, different evaluations, no editorial coordination.

The SAB also lists the second reference as "2 Samuel:22:21" with an extra colon — that's a formatting artifact in the scrape, not a real verse citation problem; the verse exists and the language is as quoted.

answers.answer_explanation:
And David's heart smote him after that he had numbered the
				          people. And David said unto the Lord, I have sinned greatly in
				          that I have done. 2 Samuel 24:10, 
				          1 Chronicles 21:8

commentary_out.commentary:
The canon answers the single question—did David sin?—in three mutually inconsistent registers. 2 Samuel 22, which is preserved almost verbatim as Psalm 18, is a royal thanksgiving hymn sung after deliverance from David's enemies. In verses 21-25 the speaker declares that the LORD "rewarded me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands he has recompensed me," and that "I was blameless before him, and I kept myself from guilt." Read at face value, this is a categorical assertion of innocence. 1 Kings 15:5, a deuteronomistic editorial summary embedded in the evaluation of a later king, gives the qualified answer: David did right "and turned not aside from anything that he commanded him all the days of his life, save only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite." And 2 Samuel 24:10, with its parallel in 1 Chronicles 21:8, has David confessing a second, distinct sin: "I have sinned greatly in that I have done" by numbering the people. Across the canon, then, the tally of David's sins is given as zero, as one, and as at least two.

The standard harmonization addresses the psalm by appeal to genre and occasion. 2 Samuel 22 is liturgical poetry, not a moral ledger, and its superscription and content tie it to David's deliverance "from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul." On this reading the "righteousness" and "clean hands" are forensic and relative: David is innocent in the specific dispute with his persecutors, especially Saul, having repeatedly spared Saul's life and refused to seize the throne by violence. There is genuine merit here. The covenant-lawsuit idiom of clean hands typically concerns a particular cause, and the psalm's setting is vindication against enemies, not a comprehensive self-assessment. Where it strains is in the unqualified diction: "according to my righteousness... the cleanness of my hands... I was blameless... I kept myself from guilt." The poem supplies no "in this matter" or "compared with Saul"; the limiting clause is supplied by the harmonizer, not the text. The most one can say is that genre softens the force of the claim without erasing its universality.

1 Kings 15:5 is harder to absorb, because it is prose and explicit. The Deuteronomistic Historian constructs David as the benchmark against whom every later Judahite king is measured, and he permits exactly one blemish on that benchmark: the Uriah affair. He does not write "save in the matter of Uriah and the census." That the census is omitted suggests either that this strand of the tradition did not reckon the census a comparable sin, or that the historian's source did not include it, or that the formula is deliberately schematic, isolating the one transgression with dynastic consequences (the sword that would not depart from David's house, 2 Sam 12:10). There is also a genuine text-critical wrinkle: the limiting clause "save only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite" is absent from part of the Greek tradition (it is lacking in Codex Vaticanus and some other LXX witnesses of 3 Reigns 15:5), which is why a number of critics treat it as a secondary expansion rather than original. That cuts against the harmonizer, not for him—on the shorter text the verse is an unqualified commendation of David with no Uriah exception at all, which only sharpens the clash with the psalm and the census, rather than a tidy single-exception formula.

The census narratives compound the problem in their own right. 2 Samuel 24:1 reports that the LORD's anger was kindled against Israel and "he incited David" to number them—the grammatical subject of the inciting is famously ambiguous (the LORD himself, or an unnamed instigator), which is part of why 1 Chronicles 21:1 recasts the inciter as "Satan" (or "an adversary," śāṭān), a theological revision in its own right. Either way both texts agree David sinned in doing it. So the very act 2 Samuel 22 would seem to exclude is confessed two chapters later in the same book.

The critical reading attributes the divergence to different hands and agendas: the psalm is inherited liturgy idealizing the king; 1 Kings 15:5 is deuteronomistic ideology fashioning a royal standard; the census account belongs to an appendix (2 Sam 21-24) of separate traditions. No editor coordinated them. (The catalogue's stray reference "2 Samuel:22:21" with the extra colon is merely a scrape artifact; the verse and its wording are as cited.) Verdict: a genuine tension that genre eases but does not dissolve, reflecting independent sources with incompatible evaluations of David.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The psalm of 2 Samuel 22 (=Psalm 18) is royal thanksgiving liturgy whose 'clean hands' language is forensic and tied to David's vindication against Saul and his enemies, so it need not be read as a comprehensive moral claim; this eases but does not remove the tension. The harder clash—1 Kings 15:5 allowing only the Uriah sin against the census of 2 Sam 24 / 1 Chr 21—is not reconciled by genre and reflects independent sources. The Uriah-exception clause is itself absent from part of the Greek tradition (Codex Vaticanus and some other LXX witnesses of 3 Reigns 15:5), and on that shorter text the verse is an unqualified commendation, which sharpens rather than resolves the tension.

entries.question: How many overseers did Solomon have?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 5:16 reports that Solomon employed 3,300 overseers over the temple workforce, while 2 Chronicles 2:18 puts the number at 3,600. The two passages describe the same administrative tier of the same building project and produce a flat numerical discrepancy of 300.
entries.commentary:
The plain reading is brutally simple. 1 Kings 5:16 (MT 5:30) says 3,300 chief officers ran the labor force. 2 Chronicles 2:18 (MT 2:17) says 3,600. Same king, same temple, same job category — different number. The Chronicler is working from a source that is essentially the Kings text and is changing it.

Apologists like Gleason Archer in the *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* try to rescue the count by claiming Kings and Chronicles are counting different supervisory tiers — that Kings excludes 300 Israelite foremen who Chronicles includes, or vice versa. The problem is that 1 Kings 5:16 and 2 Chronicles 2:18 use parallel descriptions of the same group ("those who ruled over the people that did the work"), and the harmonization requires inventing a sub-category nowhere named in either text. That is the apologist playbook, page one — postulate an unstated category whose only purpose is to absorb the numerical gap.

Critical scholarship treats this as one of dozens of small numerical drifts between the Deuteronomistic History and the Chronicler. Sara Japhet in her *I & II Chronicles* (OTL, 1993) and Steven McKenzie in the *Abingdon Old Testament Commentaries* volume on 1-2 Chronicles (2004) both note that the Chronicler systematically reshapes Solomonic numbers, often inflating them or rounding them to fit theological purposes — here likely combining the 3,300 chiefs of 1 Kings 5:16 with the 250 chief officers of 1 Kings 9:23 into a tidy 3,600 (Japhet, p. 549). It is a transmission/redaction problem, not a hidden harmony.

Verdict: this is a textbook scribal/redactional discrepancy. The harmonization works only if you invent an extra category of overseers that neither text mentions. The more parsimonious reading is that the Chronicler adjusted the figure.

				          work, three thousand and three hundred, which ruled over the

commentary_out.commentary:
The numbers sit in plain view. 1 Kings 5:16 (MT 5:30) reports 3,300 chief deputies "who ruled over the people that did the work"; 2 Chronicles 2:18 (MT 2:17) reports 3,600 overseers "to set the people to work." Same king, same temple, same administrative tier, a flat gap of 300. Because the Chronicler demonstrably works from a Vorlage essentially identical to the Kings text — the verbal parallels are close enough to rule out independent sources — the most economical description is that the Chronicler altered the figure he received.

The usual apologetic move (Gleason Archer, and before him Keil and Delitzsch) postulates two distinct supervisory grades, one of which one book counts and the other omits. Stated that loosely it looks like special pleading. But this case is stronger than most, because the supporting numbers are actually on the page rather than invented. 1 Kings tracks two figures: 3,300 chief deputies (5:16) and, in a later passage, 550 "chief officers who were over the work" (1 Kings 9:23). 2 Chronicles tracks two figures of its own: 3,600 overseers (2:18) and 250 "chief officers" (2 Chronicles 8:10). In each book the two numbers happen to sum to 3,850 — the 300 that Chronicles adds to the lower tier is exactly the 300 it drops from the upper. That equal total is a real and recognized observation, and it is the strongest form of the harmonization. But it has to be labeled for what it is. The equal sum is precisely the two-tier argument, not an independent confirmation of it: there is no statement anywhere in either book that these are partitions of one corps, and the matching total can be read just as easily as a coincidence of two divergent traditions, or as a downstream artifact of the Chronicler's own redistribution, as it can as evidence of an original single count. So the most one can say is that the books agree on a total of 3,850 supervisors while disagreeing on its internal breakdown — which softens the surface 300-discrepancy without proving the two accounts were ever a single coordinated scheme.

What remains unresolved is which partition is original and why the boundary moved. Critical scholarship situates the shift within the Chronicler's broader handling of Solomonic data. Sara Japhet (I & II Chronicles, OTL) notes that the Chronicler routinely reshapes Kings numbers, and she favors the reading that 2 Chronicles redistributes the personnel for reasons bound up with its theology of Israelite versus foreign labor — the Chronicler is careful to insist that native Israelites did not perform the servile work (2 Chronicles 8:9), which may motivate adjusting who counts as an "officer." Ralph Klein (2 Chronicles, Hermeneia) treats the figures as a transmission-and-redaction phenomenon and reviews the versional spread, where the Greek witnesses do not uniformly resolve the totals. Steven McKenzie (1-2 Chronicles, AOTC) likewise reads the Chronicler as systematically recasting the Solomonic administrative tradition rather than copying it.

The one place the simple "two tiers" harmonization can overreach is in claiming the gap proves perfect concord. It does not. Two scribal traditions can both transmit a coherent total while disagreeing about its breakdown, and a copyist confusion between similar numerals (a recurring problem in Chronicles, where letter-forms used as numerals were liable to be misread) could equally produce the same arithmetic by accident rather than design. The summed total of 3,850 is suggestive of a deliberate redistribution, but it is not decisive proof of one, since both partitions could be downstream of an earlier corruption. Mordechai Cogan (I Kings, AB 10) is appropriately cautious, treating the Kings figures as the baseline against which the Chronicler's are measured without claiming the underlying historical count is recoverable.

The upshot is that this is one of the better-behaved of the Kings-Chronicles number cases. Unlike the molten-sea volume or the pillar height, where the figures cannot be reconciled without fighting the Hebrew, here the two books at least land on the same total of 3,850 supervisors, so the surface 300-discrepancy can be recast as a difference in where the line between tiers is drawn. Verdict: partially harmonizable — but the equal-total observation is the apologetic argument restated, not an independent datum that settles it. The two accounts still report different figures for the same administrative tier, and critical scholarship leaves it genuinely undecided whether the matching sum reflects an original single corps, the Chronicler's deliberate redistribution, or a scribal accident.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The strongest harmonization (Archer; Keil-Delitzsch) rests on an equal-total observation: 1 Kings reports 3,300 chief deputies (5:16) plus 550 chief officers (1 Kings 9:23), and 2 Chronicles reports 3,600 (2:18) plus 250 (2 Chronicles 8:10) — each book summing to 3,850 supervisors. The surface 300-discrepancy can thus be recast as a difference in where the tier boundary is drawn. But the equal sum is the apologetic argument restated, not an independent datum: neither book states these are partitions of one corps, and critical scholarship (Japhet, Klein) treats the matching total as plausibly coincidental or as a product of the Chronicler's redistribution. Which partition is original, and whether a single corps ever existed, remains undecided.

entries.question: When did Solomon's reign begin?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 6:1 places Solomon's fourth regnal year — when temple construction begins — 480 years after the Exodus. Paul's speech in Acts 13:17-22, combined with the regnal data from 1 Chronicles 29:26-27, produces a total of roughly 570+ years between the Exodus and Solomon's accession, contradicting the Kings figure by about 90 years.
entries.commentary:
1 Kings 6:1 gives a precise schematic number: 480 years from the Exodus to Solomon's fourth year. Subtract the four years and you get 476 years from Exodus to accession. That is the Deuteronomistic chronology, period.

Paul in Acts 13:17-22 walks through a different chronology — 40 years in the wilderness, conquest, judges for "about 450 years," then Saul for 40 years, then David. 1 Chronicles 29:27 confirms David's 40-year reign. Add it up: 40 + an unspecified-but-real conquest period + 450 + 40 + 40 = around 570 years before you even get to Solomon's accession. The numbers don't reconcile to the 1 Kings 6:1 figure no matter how you slice it.

Apologists handle this in two main ways. The first is to argue that "about 450 years" in Acts 13:20 refers to the cumulative period from the patriarchs *through* the judges, not just the judges era — a reading promoted by F.F. Bruce in his NICNT volume on Acts. The second, championed by Eugene Merrill in *Kingdom of Priests*, is to claim 1 Kings 6:1's "480" is a symbolic 12×40 generational schema, not a literal year count. Both moves concede the obvious — that a straightforward reading produces a contradiction — and then dissolve one number into vagueness to save the other. That is post-hoc rationalization, not harmonization.

Critical scholars from Martin Noth onward treat 1 Kings 6:1 as a Deuteronomistic theological schema (12 generations of 40 years) rather than a historical datum, which is the more honest concession. Either way, Acts 13 and 1 Kings 6:1 cannot both be literally accurate chronologies of the same span. Take your pick: literal 480 from Kings and demote Paul's math, or literal Acts chronology and demote Kings as schematic.

answers.answer: 570 years after the Israelites left Egypt
answers.answer_explanation:
The God of this people of Israel chose our fathers, and exalted the people when they dwelt as strangers in the land of Egypt, and with an high arm brought he them out of it. And about the time of forty years suffered he their manners in the wilderness. And when he had destroyed seven nations in the land of Chanaan, he divided their land to them by lot. And after that he gave unto them judges about the space of four hundred and fifty years, until Samuel the prophet. And afterward they desired a king: and God gave unto them Saul the son of Cis, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, by the space of forty years. And when he had removed him, he raised up unto them David to be their king. Acts 13:17-22

Thus David the son of Jesse reigned over all Israel. And the time that he reigned over Israel was forty years; seven years reigned he in Hebron, and thirty and three years reigned he in Jerusalem. 1 Chronicles 29:26-27

commentary_out.commentary:
1 Kings 6:1 supplies a precise schematic figure: temple construction begins in Solomon's fourth year, 480 years after the Exodus — so 476 years from Exodus to Solomon's accession. This is the linchpin of the Deuteronomistic chronology. Paul's speech in Acts 13:17-22 sketches a different scheme: roughly 40 years in the wilderness, the conquest of seven nations, judges for "about 450 years" (Acts 13:20), Saul for 40 years, then David, whose 40-year reign is fixed by 1 Chronicles 29:26-27. Summed, the Acts sequence runs to roughly 570 years before Solomon's accession — a gap of about 90 years against 1 Kings 6:1.

Two apologetic strategies dominate, and each must be stated at full strength. The first, associated with F. F. Bruce, exploits a real textual problem in Acts 13:20. In the Byzantine text the "about 450 years" modifies the period of the judges; but in the earliest witnesses (P74, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus) the phrase is placed earlier and most naturally counts the 450 years from the patriarchs through the conquest — roughly 400 years of sojourn (Genesis 15:13; Exodus 12:40) plus 40 in the wilderness plus a conquest period. On that reading Acts is not stacking 450 judge-years on top of the wilderness and monarchy at all, and the apparent 570-year total evaporates. This is the strongest harmonization available and it rests on the critical text, not on special pleading. The second strategy, championed by Eugene Merrill, reads 1 Kings 6:1's "480" as a stylized twelve generations of forty years rather than a literal annual count, so that the figure was never meant to bear the precision the contradiction assumes.

Neither move, however, secures a genuine harmony of two literally accurate chronologies; each survives only by demoting one number to vagueness. The first dissolves Acts into a re-punctuation that even on its best reading yields only an approximate total, and the actual length of the conquest is left unspecified, so the "reconciliation" is a range, not a match. The second concedes outright that 1 Kings 6:1 is not a historical datum. And the deeper problem is that the 480 figure conflicts not only with Acts but with the Deuteronomistic History's own internal data: when the individual spans assigned to the judges, the oppressions, Eli, Samuel, Saul, and David are added up, they considerably exceed 480 years. Judges 11:26 has Jephthah assert that Israel had already held the land for 300 years by his day, which alone — set before Eli, Samuel, Saul, David, and Solomon's first four years — strains the 480-year envelope past breaking.

This is why critical scholarship, from Martin Noth's foundational analysis of the Deuteronomistic History onward, reads 1 Kings 6:1 as a theological-schematic construction: twelve generations of forty years marking the span from Exodus to temple, a number freighted with significance (the temple as the midpoint and telos of sacred history) rather than computed from regnal records. The Greek tradition's variant of 440 years in some witnesses (against the Hebrew's 480) confirms that the figure was already unstable in transmission and being adjusted. Mordechai Cogan (I Kings, AB 10) and Craig Keener (Acts, vol. 2) both treat the two chronologies as products of different schematizing impulses rather than competing measurements of one recoverable span.

The net result is worth stating precisely, because the two halves of this contradiction are not equally stubborn. The Acts-versus-Kings clash is the softer of the two: on the critical text of Acts 13:20, the "about 450 years" most likely counts the Egypt-plus-wilderness-plus-conquest span rather than stacking on top of the judges, so the apparent 570-year total against Kings largely evaporates, and the cross-testament discrepancy the question is built on may not be a real conflict at all. What does not go away is the tension internal to the Hebrew Bible: 1 Kings 6:1's 480 against the Deuteronomistic History's own summed spans for the judges, oppressions, Eli, Samuel, Saul, and David, with Jephthah's 300 years (Judges 11:26) alone straining the envelope. So one can save 1 Kings 6:1 as literal and treat that internal arithmetic as loose, or treat 480 as a generational symbol, but the figures cannot all be exact chronologies of the same interval. Verdict: the headline Acts-vs-Kings contradiction is largely defused on the critical text, but a genuine chronological tension survives inside the Old Testament itself, resolvable only by conceding that 1 Kings 6:1's 480 is schematic rather than a computed historical datum.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: On the critical text of Acts 13:20 (P74, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus), the 'about 450 years' most naturally counts the span from the sojourn in Egypt through the conquest (roughly 400 + 40 + a conquest period) rather than the era of the judges, so it need not be stacked on top of the wilderness and monarchy; on that reading the apparent 570-year Acts total largely evaporates and the cross-testament clash with 1 Kings 6:1 is defused. What is not harmonized is a tension internal to the Hebrew Bible: 1 Kings 6:1's 480 years conflicts with the Deuteronomistic History's own summed spans (the judges, oppressions, Eli, Samuel, Saul, David), and with Jephthah's claim of 300 years of occupation by his day (Judges 11:26). 1 Kings 6:1 is best read as a schematic twelve-generations-of-forty figure (so Noth, Cogan), and the LXX's 440-year variant at 3 Reigns 6:1 shows the number was already unstable in transmission.

entries.question: How many talents of gold did Hiram send Solomon?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 9:27-28 says Hiram's fleet brought 420 talents of gold from Ophir. 2 Chronicles 8:18 puts the figure at 450 talents. The two texts describe the same voyage, the same king, and the same gold shipment, with a 30-talent discrepancy.
entries.commentary:
Same expedition. Same Phoenician fleet. Same destination (Ophir). 1 Kings 9:28 says 420 talents. 2 Chronicles 8:18 says 450. Thirty talents of gold off — at the standard talent weight of roughly 75 pounds, that's over a ton of bullion.

Apologists have basically three options. The first, from Archer, is textual corruption: somewhere in transmission, a Hebrew numeral letter got copied wrong. This is actually the most honest harmonization, because it concedes that the texts as we have them disagree and locates the problem in scribal copying rather than in the original autographs. It also doesn't try to invent semantic categories that aren't there. The downside, for the apologist, is that admitting scribal corruption admits that the text we have is not numerically inerrant.

The second move, used in Keil-Delitzsch and J.A. Thompson's NAC 9 *1, 2 Chronicles*, is that the 30-talent gap represents shipping costs, royal commission, or some other deducted amount. Same template as every other Chronicles-Kings numerical entry — invent an unstated category to absorb the gap.

The third, less common move, is to argue Kings reports net delivered and Chronicles reports gross before loss at sea or other depletion. Same template, different label.

Critical scholars treat this with the same parsimony as the other Chronicler discrepancies. Japhet (OTL) notes that 30 is a common scribal-error candidate in Hebrew numeral letter confusion, and Klein (Hermeneia) concurs. The simplest explanation is either scribal slip or the Chronicler's habit of inflating Solomonic wealth. Take your pick — but each option concedes the texts as transmitted disagree.

answers.answer_explanation:
And Hiram sent in the navy his servants ... and they came to
			          Ophir, and fetched from thence gold, four hundred and twenty
			          talents, and brought it to Solomon. 1 Kings 9:27-28

And Huram sent him ... four hundred and fifty talents
			          of gold, and brought them to king Solomon. 2 Chronicles 8:18

commentary_out.commentary:
Both passages describe the same enterprise: Hiram (Huram) of Tyre supplies ships and crews, and the joint fleet sails to Ophir and returns with gold for Solomon. 1 Kings 9:28 gives the haul as 420 talents; 2 Chronicles 8:18 gives 450. At a talent of roughly 34 kilograms, the 30-talent gap is on the order of a metric ton of gold — not a rounding triviality in absolute terms, though a small fraction of the total.

Apologetic treatments cluster around three options. The first, which Gleason Archer himself favors here, is scribal corruption: in the course of copying, a Hebrew numeral was miscopied. This is the most candid of the harmonizations because it concedes that the texts as received disagree and locates the fault in transmission rather than in the original composition. It also avoids inventing semantic categories. Its cost, for a strict inerrantist, is the admission that the extant text is not numerically flawless. The second option, found in Keil and Delitzsch and in J. A. Thompson's NAC volume, posits an unstated deduction — shipping costs, a Tyrian commission, or losses — so that 420 is the net delivered to Solomon and 450 the gross. The third is a variant of the same: gross versus net after some attrition at sea. The second and third moves share the structural weakness of the other Chronicles-Kings numerical harmonizations: they supply a category (commission, loss) that neither verse mentions, purely to absorb the difference.

The textual-corruption explanation has the strongest evidential footing, and the mechanics are worth specifying. In the Masoretic Text these numbers are spelled out as words ('four hundred and twenty,' 'four hundred and fifty'), but the standard numeral-confusion explanation does not depend on that surface form: it posits that an earlier exemplar used a compact numerical notation — Hebrew letters or stroke-groups serving as figures, the kind of notation attested in epigraphic and later Hebrew — which a scribe could miscopy before the value was later written out in full words. That is the mechanism by which a 420 and a 450 can descend from one original, and it is exactly the kind of slip numerals are prone to, because a figure carries none of the contextual redundancy that lets a reader catch an error in an ordinary word. The Septuagint reinforces the basic point that the figure was unstable across the textual streams: Brenton's Septuagint of 3 Reigns 9:28 — the Ophir voyage verse itself, not the Queen of Sheba's gift in 1 Kings 10:10 — reads "a hundred and twenty talents of gold," a third figure that neither matches the Hebrew 420 nor the Chronicler's 450. Whether 120 is itself a corruption or an independent reckoning, its presence shows the gold total was not fixed in transmission.

Critical commentators accordingly treat the discrepancy with parsimony rather than synthesis. Sara Japhet (OTL) and Ralph Klein (Hermeneia) regard the 30-talent difference as either a copyist's slip or an instance of the Chronicler's documented tendency to enhance the wealth and grandeur of the Solomonic and Davidic monarchy (compare the Chronicler's larger figures for David's gathered gold and for temple furnishings elsewhere). On the first account the divergence is accidental; on the second it is tendentious. Either way the explanation concedes the operative point: the two texts as we have them report different totals for the same shipment, and no harmonization preserves both numbers as simultaneously, literally accurate descriptions of the gold actually delivered.

The upshot is that this is among the more easily explained discrepancies, but 'explained' is not the same as 'reconciled.' Scribal corruption is a real and probable cause; it accounts for the data better than the unstated-deduction theories; and it leaves the autographs unjudged. But it does so by granting that the transmitted text contains an error.

Verdict: harmonizable in origin (most likely scribal corruption of a numeral), but the transmitted texts genuinely disagree — a textual problem rather than a doctrinal one.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The 420/450 divergence is most economically explained as scribal corruption of a Hebrew numeral in transmission (or as the Chronicler's known tendency to round/inflate Solomonic wealth); on the textual-corruption account the autographs need not have disagreed, but the texts as transmitted do disagree.
